body:
How information travels through a communication system

Telecommunication means transmitting information over a distance through an electrical, optical or electromagnetic system. The information may be speech, text, images, video or computer data. A basic communication system contains a transmitter, a communication channel and a receiver.

The transmitter converts information into a suitable signal and sends it through the channel. The channel may be an optical fibre, a copper cable or free space. The receiver detects the arriving signal and reconstructs the information. During transmission, noise, interference and signal weakening may reduce its quality.

Radio waves are electromagnetic waves

Radio waves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum. This distinguishes them from sound waves, which are mechanical waves and require a material medium such as air, water or a solid.

A mobile phone transmits radio-frequency electromagnetic signals. It does not send ordinary sound waves directly to a distant mobile tower. Its microphone first converts speech into an electrical or digital representation that the radio equipment can transmit.

Frequency, wavelength and bandwidth

Frequency is the number of complete wave cycles occurring in 1 second. Its unit is the hertz (Hz). A kilohertz (kHz) is 1,000 Hz, a megahertz (MHz) is 1,000,000 Hz, and a gigahertz (GHz) is 1,000,000,000 Hz.

Wavelength is the distance between corresponding points of successive waves. For electromagnetic waves travelling through the same medium, frequency and wavelength are inversely related: a higher frequency has a shorter wavelength.

Different frequencies have different practical propagation characteristics. Lower-frequency radio signals can often provide wider coverage and better penetration around some obstacles. Higher-frequency bands can provide substantial communication capacity when sufficiently wide channels are available, but may face shorter practical coverage, greater obstruction losses or more demanding deployment conditions. Actual performance also depends on equipment, terrain, transmitted power and network design.

A higher radio frequency does not automatically mean a higher internet speed. Data speed depends on several factors, including available channel bandwidth, signal quality, modulation, coding, network congestion and equipment capabilities.

The term bandwidth has 2 related but different uses. In radio engineering, it describes the width of a frequency band and is measured in Hz. In everyday internet usage, it often refers loosely to a connection's data-carrying capacity. The actual data rate is normally expressed in bits per second (bps), not Hz.

What is radio spectrum management?

The radio-frequency spectrum is the range of radio frequencies available for wireless communication. Radio and television broadcasting, mobile networks, satellite services and other wireless systems use parts of this spectrum.

Different transmitters operating without suitable coordination may cause harmful interference. Governments therefore regulate radio-spectrum use, while the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) coordinates international frequency allocations and related rules. Article 5 of the ITU Radio Regulations contains the international Table of Frequency Allocations.

Some frequency bands are used under individual spectrum licences or assignments, while others permit specified equipment to operate without an individual spectrum licence, subject to technical conditions. Unlicensed operation does not mean unregulated operation. The permitted uses and conditions vary between countries.

Modulation carries information on a radio wave

A carrier wave is a comparatively regular electromagnetic wave used to transport information. Modulation changes a property of this carrier according to the information being transmitted. The receiver performs the corresponding detection or demodulation to recover the information.

  • Amplitude modulation (AM): the amplitude of the carrier changes according to the information signal. Its frequency remains approximately constant in the simplest explanation.
  • Frequency modulation (FM): the instantaneous frequency of the carrier varies according to the information signal, while its amplitude is kept approximately constant in the idealised system.
  • Digital modulation: the transmitter represents digital information through selected changes in a carrier's amplitude, frequency, phase or a combination of these properties.

AM and FM describe methods of conveying information; they do not by themselves indicate whether the message is private. Modulation prepares information for transmission, whereas encryption protects information against unauthorised reading.

Prelims focus

  • Radio waves and light are electromagnetic waves; sound is a mechanical wave.
  • Electromagnetic waves can propagate through a vacuum.
  • Frequency is measured in Hz; digital data rate is measured in bps.
  • AM varies carrier amplitude; FM varies carrier frequency.
  • ITU Radio Regulations, Article 5, contains the international Table of Frequency Allocations.
  • Trap: Modulation is not the same as encryption, and an unlicensed band is not free from technical rules.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, ch. 12, 'Sound', printed pp. 160–164, 2018–19 edition; ITU Radiocommunication Bureau, 'Frequently Asked Questions', entries I002–I006 and Article 5 references, consulted 4 November 2026; ITU, Radio Regulations, international frequency-allocation framework, consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
Why a mobile network is called cellular

A cellular network divides its coverage area into many smaller geographical service areas called cells. Each cell is served by radio equipment at a base station or related radio site. A mobile device communicates over radio with an appropriate base station, while the wider network connects it to other users and services.

Cells are not necessarily perfect hexagons in reality. Their coverage depends on geography, buildings, antenna placement, signal strength and traffic demand. Hexagonal shapes are commonly used in simplified explanations because they help illustrate coverage and frequency reuse.

Frequency reuse

Radio spectrum is limited. Cellular networks improve its use by permitting suitably separated cells to reuse the same frequency resources while managing interference. This principle is called frequency reuse. It allows a network to serve many users over a large area without requiring a completely new set of frequencies for every cell.

Where more people need service, operators may increase capacity by adding radio sites, using available spectrum more efficiently or deploying additional frequency resources. However, cells close to one another must coordinate their transmissions to limit interference.

Handover between cells

When a person moves during a call or data session, the serving cell may become unsuitable. The network can transfer the connection to another cell through a process called handover or handoff. Successful handover helps maintain service while the user moves.

The radio connection from a device to a base station is the access link. The connection carrying traffic from the radio site towards the operator's wider network is called backhaul. Backhaul frequently uses optical fibre, but microwave radio and other links are also possible.

Cellular generations and their main characteristics

GenerationMain developmentRecognition facts
1GAnalogue cellular voiceEarly mobile telephone systems; primarily voice service.
2GDigital cellular communicationDigital voice and SMS; GSM is a prominent 2G system.
3GImproved mobile dataMore practical internet access and multimedia communication.
4GMobile broadband using packet-based networksLTE family; substantially improved internet and video services.
5GEnhanced mobile broadband and support for new application requirements5G New Radio (NR); potential for higher capacity, lower latency and large numbers of connected devices.

The generations indicate major developments in network capability; they are not merely labels for successive increases in download speed. Digital voice, mobile internet, network efficiency and the ability to support different types of devices have changed over successive generations.

ITU terminology

The ITU uses the name International Mobile Telecommunications (IMT) for families of mobile telecommunication standards. Important associations are IMT-2000 with 3G, IMT-Advanced with 4G and IMT-2020 with 5G. These are standards frameworks rather than names of individual mobile operators.

5G NR means 5G New Radio. A 5G network may initially operate with support from existing 4G infrastructure, or it may use a 5G standalone architecture. The presence of 5G radio coverage alone does not guarantee a particular application will experience extremely low delay.

Three ideas often associated with 5G

  • Enhanced mobile broadband: faster and more capable mobile data services, including high-quality video and large data transfers.
  • Ultra-reliable and low-latency communications (URLLC): the ability to support applications that require rapid responses, provided the whole system is appropriately designed.
  • Massive machine-type communication: support for many connected sensors and other devices that exchange relatively small amounts of data.

Latency means the time taken for information to travel through a communication path and produce the relevant response. A high data rate and a low latency are different characteristics. A connection may transfer large files quickly but still have noticeable delay during an interactive activity.

India's 5G milestone and the status of 6G

Commercial 5G services were formally launched in India on 1 October 2022. This is a historical launch date, not a statement that every location immediately received 5G coverage.

The next IMT framework is IMT-2030, commonly associated with 6G. As of the content cutoff of 4 November 2026, international requirements and evaluation work for IMT-2030 were still progressing. Accordingly, 6G should not be treated as an already established nationwide commercial cellular generation in India. India's Bharat 6G Vision was released on 22 March 2023 as a development vision, not as a declaration of completed 6G deployment.

Prelims focus

  • 1G used analogue cellular voice; 2G introduced digital cellular communication.
  • GSM is associated with 2G; LTE is associated with the 4G family; NR is associated with 5G.
  • IMT-2000, IMT-Advanced and IMT-2020 correspond to 3G, 4G and 5G respectively.
  • Handover transfers a continuing connection between serving cells.
  • India launched 5G services on 1 October 2022.
  • Trap: IMT-2030 represents the development of 6G standards, not proof that 6G is already commercially available everywhere.

[Sources: ITU Radiocommunication Sector, 'Detailed Information about the IMT-family', IMT-2000, IMT-Advanced, IMT-2020 and IMT-2030 sections, consulted 4 November 2026; ITU-R Working Party 5D, 'IMT towards 2030 and beyond', development status, consulted 4 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Communications, 'Prime Minister Launches 5G Services in India', 1 October 2022; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Communications, 'Introduction of 6G Spectrum Technology', 12 March 2025.]

pictures.caption: Handover allows a moving device to continue communicating through a more suitable cell.

title: Cellular Mobile Networks: Cells, Handover and Generations from 1G to 5G

body:
Why long-distance networks use different transmission media

A telecommunications network must carry information between local users, exchanges, data centres and distant regions. A wireless connection is useful for mobility, but much of the wider network may use physical cables. Optical fibre and satellite links are important technologies for carrying communication over distance.

Both may transport digital data, but they use different paths. Optical fibre guides light through a cable, whereas a satellite link uses radio-frequency electromagnetic waves travelling between Earth stations and a satellite.

Optical fibre: information carried by light

An optical fibre is a very thin strand of transparent material, generally glass, that guides light along its length. Information is represented through changes in the transmitted optical signal. The receiver detects the arriving light and converts the information into a usable electrical or digital form.

A typical optical fibre has a central core surrounded by cladding. The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding. This structure confines and guides light in the core. At school level, the guiding principle is explained using total internal reflection.

Total internal reflection occurs when light travelling in an optically denser medium meets the boundary with a less optically dense medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. Instead of passing through that boundary as a refracted ray, the light is reflected back into the denser medium. Modern fibre propagation is more fully described using electromagnetic-wave behaviour, but total internal reflection gives the essential school-level explanation.

Why optical fibre is widely used

  • High capacity: optical systems can carry very large quantities of information.
  • Low attenuation: suitable fibre systems can transmit information over long distances with relatively low signal loss.
  • Resistance to electromagnetic interference: light in a glass fibre is not disturbed by ordinary external electrical interference in the same way as a metallic conductor.
  • Backhaul and backbone use: fibre can connect mobile towers, exchanges, towns, Gram Panchayats and data centres.

Fibre is not immune to all failures. Excavation, accidental cuts, damaged connectors, poor installation and equipment faults can interrupt a fibre network. A cable also requires physical installation, which can be difficult in some remote or mountainous locations.

Satellite communication: the uplink and downlink

A communication satellite acts as a relay between locations on Earth. A transmitting Earth station sends a signal to the satellite through an uplink. A satellite transponder receives the signal, performs the required processing such as amplification and frequency conversion, and retransmits it towards an Earth station through a downlink.

Communication satellites can support television broadcasting, telephone services, internet links and connectivity where installing terrestrial communication lines is difficult. India uses the INSAT/GSAT satellite families for communication and related services. Remote-sensing satellites are principally used for observing Earth rather than acting as ordinary telephone or internet relays. A satellite's role must therefore be identified from its mission, not merely from the fact that it orbits Earth.

Geostationary and low-Earth-orbit satellites

A geostationary satellite occupies a circular equatorial orbit approximately 35,786 km above Earth's surface and moves in the direction of Earth's rotation at the matching angular speed. It therefore appears fixed over one longitude. This makes continuous communication coverage possible over a broad region using suitably directed ground antennas.

A low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite travels much closer to Earth and does not ordinarily remain fixed over one point on the ground. A network of many LEO satellites can provide continuing coverage as individual satellites move into and out of view.

The shorter signal path of a LEO connection can reduce propagation delay compared with a geostationary connection. However, overall service quality also depends on network routing, ground equipment, traffic and the satellite system. Neither orbit type guarantees uninterrupted internet service by itself.

Comparing fibre and satellite links

FeatureOptical fibreSatellite link
Signal mediumLight guided in a physical cableRadio waves travelling through space
Typical strengthHigh-capacity terrestrial backboneWide-area or remote-location connectivity
Important limitationCable installation and physical damagePropagation delay, visibility and radio-link conditions
Common applicationMobile backhaul and broadband networksBroadcasting and remote communication links

Prelims focus

  • Optical fibre carries information using light, an electromagnetic wave.
  • The core and cladding have different refractive indices; total internal reflection explains guiding at school level.
  • A satellite uplink travels from Earth towards the satellite; a downlink travels from the satellite towards Earth.
  • A geostationary orbit is about 35,786 km above the equator.
  • INSAT/GSAT are associated with communication services.
  • Trap: A wireless mobile phone can still depend on optical fibre for the network's backhaul.

[Sources: Corning Optical Communications, 'Optical Fiber Glossary of Terms', entries 'Core and Cladding' and 'Total Internal Reflection', consulted 4 November 2026; ISRO, 'FAQ Communication', questions 1–3 on communication satellites and transponders, consulted 4 November 2026; NOAA, 'Weather Satellites', geostationary orbit section, consulted 4 November 2026; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, ch. 10, 'Transport and Communication', printed pp. 122–123, satellite communication section.]
